November 2009 # Betting on China - Chinese imports kept the market ex-China in deficit in Q2 and Q3. However, the SHFE-LME arbitrage has been closed for several months and we expect Chinese imports to fall from the surprisingly strong September figure. - The market ex-China should, given lower Chinese imports and continued q-o-q increases in refined output, move into a modest surplus in Q4. This is already apparent in the continued build up in LME and COMEX stocks over the past month. - Copper prices have stayed strong thus far in Q4, with official prices averaging $6,267/t in October (to the 28th ). In the last three years, prices have fallen q-o-q in Q4. Investor momentum should support prices this year, but we believe that the slight easing of market tightness will see prices soften from current levels of around $6,500/t. |The supply/demand

The copper price held to an upward trajectory in October, with 3-month prices rising from a two-month low of $5,814/t on 5th October to a high of $6,765/t on 26th October before softening slightly to an official price of $6,505/t on 28th October.

This is in the context of a global market that we estimate is heading for a surplus of almost 300,000t in Q4.  On the face of it, the market appears to have moved further ahead of fundamentals, which poses several questions.  On a pro-rata basis our estimate of the Q4 surplus in October is almost 100,000t.  Exchange stocks have risen by only a little over 16,000t since the start of October to reach more than 500,000t currently.  Where has the rest of the tonnage ended up?  It is clear that investors are taking an interest in the market.  What effect is investor interest having on prices, and at what point could investor money leave the market?  Finally, if prices have indeed moved ahead of fundamentals, could fundamentals catch up, or will prices fall? 

## **Chinese imports keep the market tight** 

Much of this year‟s price movement can be accounted for by the impact of the build up of inventory in China on the world ex-China.  This build-up included restocking by the State Reserve Bureau (SRB), which we now estimate at only 160,000t, but also purchases by fabricators and merchants, right down to very small investors (Chinese state television mentioned pig farmers).  CRU estimates that this invisible stock build (excluding the SRB) could be in the region of 500,000-600,000t, facilitated by record levels of liquidity in China, and by the fact that copper is relatively easy to store. 

There was a surprising 28.7% month-on-month increase of Chinese imports of refined copper in September to 282,828t.  Given the closure of the SHFE-LME arbitrage and the recent declining trend in the spot premium, we do not believe that this was a reflection of an acceleration in domestic demand or the start of a new bout of stock building.  We suspect the increase in imports in September may have been due to shipments booked earlier this year, and possibly some additional financing of copper by market insiders who were worried about potential credit tightening in August.  Chinese exports of refined copper rose to their highest level this year in September – 10,705t – more than in the whole first half of the year.  This was most likely bonded warehouse material.  We do not see this increase in exports as the start of a significant flow of metal from China, as we expect Chinese demand for refined material will be sufficient to keep metal in the country.  Nonetheless, export figures certainly bear watching in the months ahead. 

The build up of inventory in China put the market outside of China in deficit in Q2, leading to a rundown in LME stocks.  Although Chinese imports slowed in Q3, they remained sufficiently high to keep the market ex-China in modest deficit.  However, we expect that the market ex-China will move into a small surplus in Q4.  LME prices remain above $6,000/t, indicating that the market appears to believe that most of the excess material accumulated this year will stay in China.  Currently, with credit easy to obtain, most Chinese investors seem t

o have adequate levels of cash, so are unlikely to feel pressured to sell their material quickly. In addition, physical traders storing stock in bonded warehouses seem to have been able to secure inexpensive financing from banks, reducing the opportunity cost of holding metal. ## **Investment money favours copper** With the economic downturn appearing to have hit bottom, risk appetite has returned, with copper attracting its share for several reasons. There has been a general interest in dollar-denominated commodities as a hedge against inflation. Industrial commodities have also been attractive ahead of the anticipated recovery in manufacturing demand. However, copper has also been relatively more attractive to investors than some other commodities because the market has been perceived as relatively tight this year. Much of this perceived tightness has been a result of major stock building in China and the impact on the market balance ex-China, as detailed above. © 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 2 of 12 Copper Monitor November 2009 www.crumonitor.com Positions held by index funds

Most of this investment in copper appears to be relatively long term, based on the perception that market tightness in copper will continue. Data compiled by CRU‟s Price Risk Management division points to a large rebound in index fund investment in copper this year, which tends to take more passive long-term positions. It is possible for investors to shift positions, but in order for them to move from a „buy/hold‟ bias to a „sell‟ bias and push prices lower, they need to see some very bad news on either the global economy or copper demand. In the absence of that, this money is likely to remain supportive of copper prices. COMEX market data for the new “managed money” category, which includes both CTAs and hedge funds, also points to an ongoing shift from “short” positions to “long” positions. ## **Supply-side factors bullish for price** The copper price may have more than doubled since the start of the year, but the supply-side response has been reasonably **3008-Jan-08 13-May-08 16-Sep-08 20-Jan-09 26-May-09** muted. Although high prices have prevented further cutbacks Data: CRU Price Risk Management in mine production, few of the closures and cutbacks made in late 2008/early 2009 have yet to be brought back on-stream. Overall, CRU believes that concentrate mine production in 2009 will be down 2.8% y-o-y and refined production down 3.9% y-o-y (with depressed scrap availability being an additional factor, offsetting an improvement in EW cathode production). The contraction in mine production is despite around 474,000t (when fully operat

ional) of new mine capacity having come on-stream this year. 

Supply remains constrained due to ongoing problems and limited additional capacity that is able to swing back if prices rally.  Furthermore, mines and projects continue to be vulnerable to technical (e.g Olympic Dam), political (e.g. DR Congo mines) and labour (e.g. Spence) disruptions.  Notably, the reported problems with the main shaft at BHP Billiton‟s Olympic Dam underground mine, which have caused it to declare _force majeure_ on some shipments for next year, with the mine expected to operate at 25% of capacity until March 2010. 

## **High prices encourage strike action, strike action encourages high prices** 

As prices have risen so have the risks of strike action by workers looking to secure their share of higher revenues.  In turn, talk of strike action is helping maintain high prices.  Mines with pending negotiations for collective labour agreements account for 20% of copper production in Chile.  Disruption from industrial action is recurrent in Chile, due to labour legislation that includes strike action if an agreement has not been reached after a certain number of days.  Recently, discussions to end a 16-day strike at BHP Billiton's Spence mine in Chile have failed to reach a deal.  The union is reported to have demanded similar to the deal agreed for Escondida (operated by BHP Billiton); which is the most generous ever seen in Chile. We consider these issues in depth in our **Copper South America Report** , also released today. 

## **Demand shows few signs of improvement** 

There has been little change to the demand picture since last month.  Indications are that physical demand is remaining stable after its rally in Q2 from the depths of the downturn in Q1.  However, there are few signs that it is accelerating into a full-blooded recovery.  An initial review of the first batch of third quarter financial statements released by major fabricating companies and wire and cablemakers offers few signs of a fundamental improvement in market conditions.  Third quarter production was negatively affected by longer summer holiday shutdowns.  The automotive sector (wiring, harnesses, and some flat rolled products) is the

For the most part, the power sector and some speciality industry segments (e.g. oil and gas, mass transit) continue to perform well, but there is little evidence of a broadbased sequential improvement in North American or European markets.  Underlying refined demand in China remains robust but has also seen little improvement recently. 

Spot cathode premiums in Europe remain steady at $50-60/t on what little business is being transacted, as traders report that activity remains minimal.  There has been a

However, there remains considerable uncertainty. Growth so far has largely been propelled by stimulus packages and, in China, credit easing. As governments seek to unwind these packages, there are considerable question marks over the ability of other sectors of the economy (consumers, exporters) to pick up the slack on a self-sustaining basis. Furthermore, the financial sector remains fragile, with further consumer spending constrained in the developed world by rising unemployment and debt repayment threatening more loan defaults, which would put continued pressure on bank balance sheets. Key end-use sectors for copper, such as construction, will also face ongoing difficulties in industrialised markets. ## **Dating, not mating** Typically, contracted copper purchases for next year are often agreed in the „mating season‟ at LME week or at the American Copper Council‟s meeting in mid-November. However, we understand that few contracts have been finalised so far this year. Consumers remain uncertain about how much copper they will need in the year ahead. Reports suggest that Codelco‟s benchmark European annual premium will remain at $80/t. The outlook for Asian premiums remains uncertain. It is thought that they could rise by $10-15/t to $85-90/t next year in anticipation of an increase in demand led by a global economic recovery, with premiums further supported by the strength of Chinese consumption. However, on the downside, Chinese cathode imports are likely to fall next year due to lower scrap replacement of cathodes and no SRB buying. In addition, some invisible stocks in China are likely to make their way onto the market, especially if the central bank begins tightening monetary policy. All of the above gives consumers good reason to pause before committing to take too much refined copper next year. ## **Chinese stocks remain the swing factor** Investor interest and the weakening of the dollar have supported the copper price into the fourth quarter. Overall, in the world excluding China, the average annual growth was only 0.5% per year over the period. Production in Europe and the Rest of the World both maintained slightly above average growth to roughly preserve share. This growth was almost completely offset by the 3.5% average annual decline in North East Asia (particularly Japan and Korea) and the Americas (mostly North America) combined. ## **Production of wirerod in developed world hit hardest by the recession** Global production of wirerod is expected to decline by 6.3% in 2009, following a 1.0% increase in 2008. The 2009 decline should be slightly less than the anticipated 6.7% fall in consumption, as stocks were run down last year during the onset of the recession in Q4. The outcome had been predicted to be much worse earlier in the year, but this has been avoided by an expected 9.6% increase in Chinese production (from 3.8M tonnes to 4.2M tonnes) in response to the government stimulus for demand from the wire and cable industry and amplified by market share gains from imported rod. By contrast, copper wirerod production in the world excluding China is forecast to fall by 12.1% from 10.5M tonnes to 9.3M tonnes in 2009. The regional pattern of this contraction shows that, in addition to China, only South Korea, India, the Middle East and Africa should see an increase in production this year. As for the rest of the world, the worst affected region by the 2009 economic recession on wirerod production has been Europe (-20.3%), with both Western (-18.0%) and Eastern & Central Europe (-24.5%) hit hard. North America (and Canada in particular), Japan and Taiwan make up the rest o

f the producing countries/regions that have suffered the severest declines in production in the current downturn. South Korean wirerod production is forecast to grow by 18.3% this year. This result has been one of the more surprising especially compared to Japan and Taiwan, which are expected to see declines in 2009 of 20% and 11.4% respectively. South Korean wirerod consumption is on course to rebound by 15% in 2009 making good the 14.7% decline last year. Production of both will be affected and CRU currently forecasts the full year 2009 production will be 143,000t of electro-refined copper cathodes and 10,000t SXEW copper cathodes.  2010 production is forecast to be 155,000t of electro-refined copper cathodes and 10,000t of SXEW copper cathodes.  BHP Billiton has not yet established the full scale of the damage so these figures are subject to change. 

- The strike at **BHP Billiton’s Spence** SXEW mine in Chile continues, reducing production to a minimum.  The strike began on 13<sup>th</sup> October and has continued since then.  The 560 unionised workers are targeting a 5.5% wage increase from their 2006 contract which expired at the end of September.  This is the first collective contract negotiation to occur at Spence since the mine started up in 2006.  CRU forecasts Spence to produce around 161,000t of copper cathodes this year. 

- In contrast to its Spence operation, it was reported that an early offer by **BHP Billiton** to workers at the **Escondida** mine, in advance of the collective labour negotiations, was accepted.  The proposal includes a 5% wage increase, plus bonuses and benefits.  The agreement was reached on 13<sup>th</sup> October, but the contract was not due to expire until 5<sup>th</sup> December.  In 2009, Escondida is expected to produce 744,000t of copper-in-concentrates and 332,000t of SXEW copper cathode. 

- An early offer by **Codelco** to miners at **Andina** was, however, rebuffed at the beginning of October, with the miners saying they would prefer to negotiate during that set negotiating period at the end of the contract.  The contract is due to expire at the end of November.  CRU forecasts Andina will produce 218,000t of copper-in-concentrates in 2009, subject to no strike action during the negotiating period. 

- In early October, the **Chilean National Congress** approved a bill to revamp the corporate structure of the state-owned **Codelco** to make its operations more like a private company – though it will remain state owned.  It is hoped this will allow Codelco to increase copper production which has stagnated over the last few years.  In addition, the company will receive a US$1B grant for investment, as part of a government economic stimulus package.  Codelco is currently working on projects to expand production at **Andina** and **El Teniente** and extend the mine life at **Salvador, El Teniente** and **Chuquicamata** . 

- The re-start of **Comibol’s Corocoro** mine in Bolivia was finalised on the 26<sup>th</sup> October with an official opening ceremony by President Evo Morales.  The SXEW mine, which closed in the 1980s, was re-started following investment from South Korean state natural resources company, **Kores** , and currently has a capacity of 12,000t/y of copper cathode production.  Comibol recently announced plans to expa

nd production to around 30,000-50,000t/y of copper cathodes.

## **Exploration and Development** 









- **Freeport-McMoRan Copper and Gold** confirmed it put plans to extend the life of the **El Abra** mine in Chile back on track.  CRU forecasts the extended operation will have a capacity of around 148,000t/y of copper cathodes and will operate from 2012. 

- On 6<sup>th</sup> October, **Rio Tinto** and **Ivanhoe Mines** signed an agreement with the Government of Mongolia over the **Oyu Tolgoi** copper-gold project.  The government will have an equity stake of 34% with the balance held by Ivanhoe Mines.  Following the deal Rio Tinto purchased a further 9.95% stake in Ivanhoe Minerals, for US$388M, taking its share to 19.9%.  CRU forecasts the Oyu Tolgoi project will start up in 2013 and produce around 436,000 t/y of copper-in-concentrates. 

- **Xstrata** made several announcements regarding copper projects over the last month.  These include the sale of its 70% stake in the **El Morro** copper project in Chile to **Barrick Gold** for around US$465M; plans to extend the life of its **Lomas Bayas** mine by eight years from 2012; and a 4.5% increase in contained copper resource at its **Tampakan** project in the Philippines.  CRU forecasts the El Morro project to start up in 2013 and have a production capacity of 150,000t/y of copper-inconcentrates.  CRU forecasts Tampakan will not start up until beyond 2015, but once operating it could have a capacity of around 340,000t/y of copper-in-concentrates.  The extension of Lomas Bayas will maintain production at 70,000t/y of copper cathode, for a cost of US$293M. 

- **Konkola Copper Mines (KCM)** (a subsidiary of **Vedanta Resources** ) confirmed it plans to invest US$10M in reclaiming copper from the **Chingola** mine tailings, in Zambia.  The company hopes the Chingola operation will produce around 24,000t/y of extra copper cathodes.  CRU currently forecasts this project will start up in 2012. 

## **Smelting and Refining** 







- **Pan Pacific Copper** will shut its **Saganoseki** plant for regular maintenance throughout November. Pan Pacific Copper operates the **Hitachi** and Saganoseki smelters in Japan with a combined production capacity of 460,000t/y of copper cathodes. 

- The **Chambishi** smelter in Zambia announced that it plans to double its production capacity to nearly 300,000t/y of blister copper in 2010. Chambishi is a joint venture between **China Non-ferrous Metals Corporation (CNMC)** and **Yunnan Copper** .  The smelter plans to source raw materials from **NFC Africa** (a subsidiary of CNMC), **First Quantum Mineral’s Kansanshi** mine, **Equinox Mineral’s Lumwana** mine and **Metorex’s Chibuluma** mine, all in Zambia. 

- **Konkola Copper Mines (KCM)** (a subsidiary of **Vedanta Resources** ) confirmed that its **Nchanga** smelter in Zambia was now operating a

t full capacity following a maintenance closure in September. The smelter has a production capacity of 250,000t/y of blister copper.  CRU forecasts 70,000t of blister copper output this year, as it ramps up to full production and also deals with technical issues. 

## **Consumption** 



- **Nexans** published its Q3 2009 sales results and announced that revenues amounted to US$1.90 billion, down by 25% y-o-y.  At constant metal prices this corresponds to a 19% y-o-y organic decrease.  For the nine months to September Nexans reported a 17% y-o-y organic fall in its cable business, compared to a 16% y-o-y contraction experienced in H1.  Lower building cable sales in Europe and Asia-Pacific, as well as setbacks in the execution of high voltage contracts affected sales.

- It was reported that the Chinese copper wire producer **TCICO, Tianjin** has commissioned its second CONTIROD continuous copper wirerod plant.  The project has annual production capacity of 150,000t of rolled wirerod. **SMS Meer** supplied the technical equipment of the project.  The investment is part of the **Tianjin Pipe Corp. Group** strategy to expand its production capacity and increase its share in the growing copper wirerod market. 



- According to data released by the **Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers’ Association** , 

- Japanese copper wire and cable offtake in September contracted by 17% y-o-y, the 12th sequential monthly decrease.  Shipments in September amounted to an estimated 57,800t, a 14% m-o-m increase.  As a result, the copper wire and cable sales forecast for FY2009 has been revised down to 648,000t compared to an earlier projection of 705,000t.  In addition, the **Japan Copper and Brass Association** said that copper semis output in Japan fell by 17% y-o-y to 66,145t in September.  But from a m-o-m perspective, September rose by 5%, the sixth consecutive monthly improvement.  It is expected that demand in FY2009 will amount to 713,930t; that will be the lowest level since FY1975 and will represent an 11% contraction compared with FY2008. 



- **Cerro Flow Products, KobeWieland Copper Products, Mueller Copper Tube Products** and **Mueller Copper Tube** have petitioned the US government to impose anti-dumping duties on Chinese and Mexican imports of copper tube.  The petitioners requested a dumping margin of 60.6% for Chinese and 54.1% for Mexican exporters.  It was claimed that supported by price cuts, the exporters managed to raise their market share by 5.4% between 2006 and 2009 whilst the four US fabricators lost 4.4%.  The four petitioners account for 55.6% of total US production of seamless copper tube.
